title: Global Admin on a non-compliant device
summary: A Global Administrator signs in from an unmanaged, non-compliant computer, giving an attacker on that machine full control of the tenant.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: An attacker controls a personal, unmanaged computer that a Global Administrator uses, and has the admin's password and MFA approval.

steps.title: Sign-in evaluated by Conditional Access
steps.text: The admin account signs in from the unmanaged Windows machine. Only a device requirement can tell this machine apart from a trusted one.

gaps.text: Admins are not required to use a compliant device, so any machine can hold an admin session.

fix.caTemplate: Require a compliant device for administrators

steps.whenFixed: Blocked: administrators must use a compliant device, so the unmanaged machine cannot hold the session.

steps.title: Admin portals opened
steps.text: The attacker opens the admin centers and reviews users, roles and licensing. Nothing is changed yet, so the session looks like routine administration.
steps.whenFixed: A shorter idle timeout ends the abandoned admin session before it can be misused.

steps.title: New administrator created
steps.text: The attacker adds a second account to a privileged role so access survives a password reset. This creates a standing back door into the tenant.
steps.whenFixed: The role change is written to the audit log and surfaces for review.

outcome.prevented: The admin session is refused on the unmanaged device, so the attacker never reaches the admin centers.
outcome.notPrevented: The attacker gains lasting tenant-wide control through a hidden second administrator.

title: Anyone link on a sensitive site
summary: An attacker creates an Anyone link on a sensitive SharePoint site so files can be downloaded without signing in.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker controls an account with access to a sensitive site and wants to move data out with as little friction as possible.

steps.title: Anyone link created
steps.text: The attacker creates an Anyone link that grants access to files without any sign-in. The link can be shared or sold freely.
steps.whenFixed: Anonymous sharing is disabled, so no Anyone link can be created, and the attempt is recorded.

steps.title: Files downloaded through the link
steps.text: Anyone holding the link downloads the files without authenticating. There is no record of who took the data.
steps.whenFixed: A short expiry on Anyone links narrows the window in which the link works.

outcome.prevented: Anonymous sharing is refused, so a no-sign-in link is never created.
outcome.notPrevented: Sensitive files are downloadable by anyone who receives the link.

title: Silent tenant: auditing turned off
summary: With the Unified Audit Log disabled, an attacker acts inside the tenant knowing that key actions leave no usable trail.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker has taken over an account and finds that the Unified Audit Log is turned off. Actions will not be recorded for later investigation.

steps.title: No audit trail confirmed
steps.text: The attacker confirms that sign-ins and admin actions are not being logged. This removes the main record responders would rely on.
steps.whenFixed: The Unified Audit Log is on, so every following action is recorded for investigation.

steps.title: Mailbox read without a trace
steps.text: The attacker opens the mailbox and searches for valuable mail. With mailbox auditing off, the access leaves little evidence.
steps.whenFixed: Mailbox auditing records the access even when the attacker expects silence.

steps.title: Mail forwarded out
steps.text: The attacker adds a rule that forwards new mail to an external address, assuming the change will go unseen.
steps.whenFixed: External forwarding is blocked and, with the audit log on, the rule creation raises an alert.

outcome.prevented: With auditing on, every step is recorded and the forwarding rule is blocked and alerted.
outcome.notPrevented: The attacker reads and forwards mail with almost no trace left behind.

title: Bulk sync to an unmanaged device
summary: A compromised user syncs entire document libraries to a personal, unmanaged computer, copying company data off managed systems.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker controls a user's account and signs in from a personal, unmanaged computer to collect data.

steps.title: Sign-in evaluated by Conditional Access
steps.text: The attacker connects the OneDrive client from an unmanaged Windows machine. Only an unmanaged-device control can limit what the sync client can pull.

gaps.text: Access from unmanaged devices is not restricted, so the sync client can copy whole libraries.

fix.caTemplate: Block downloads on unmanaged devices for SharePoint and OneDrive

steps.whenFixed: Blocked: unmanaged devices are limited to web-only access, so the sync client cannot download.

steps.title: Libraries copied to the local disk
steps.text: The attacker syncs entire libraries to the personal machine, pulling documents off managed systems. The data now sits outside the tenant's controls.
steps.whenFixed: The sync button is disabled and the copied data is limited by sync restrictions.

outcome.prevented: Unmanaged devices are held to web-only access, so libraries cannot be synced off.
outcome.notPrevented: Whole libraries land on a personal machine beyond the reach of tenant controls.

title: Device-code phishing
summary: An attacker tricks a user into approving a device-code sign-in and receives a fully authenticated token that already includes the MFA claim.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker starts a device-code sign-in and sends the code to the user with a convincing message. The user enters the code and approves it.

steps.title: Sign-in evaluated by Conditional Access
steps.text: The device-code flow completes and hands the attacker a token that already satisfies MFA. Only a policy that blocks this flow can stop it.

gaps.text: Device code flow is not blocked, so a phished code becomes a working token.

steps.whenFixed: Blocked: device code flow is refused, so the phished code cannot become a token.

steps.title: Token used to read mail and files
steps.text: The attacker uses the token to read the user's mailbox and documents. The traffic looks like a normal signed-in app.
steps.whenFixed: Mailbox auditing records the access even though the sign-in looked legitimate.

steps.title: Inbox rule created for ongoing reach
steps.text: The attacker adds an inbox rule to keep receiving the user's mail. This keeps a copy flowing after the token expires.
steps.whenFixed: The rule creation raises an alert and external delivery is blocked.

outcome.prevented: The device-code sign-in is refused, so the phished code is useless.
outcome.notPrevented: The attacker reads mail and files and sets up an inbox rule to keep access.

title: Guest re-share sprawl
summary: A guest re-shares files they were given, spreading access to more outsiders than the owner intended.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: A guest was shared a folder for a project and can re-share it. The attacker controls that guest account.

steps.title: Files re-shared to more outsiders
steps.text: The guest shares the files onward to additional external people. Access now reaches people the owner never approved.
steps.whenFixed: External users cannot re-share, so access does not spread beyond the owner's intent.

steps.title: Access spreads beyond control
steps.text: Each new recipient can potentially share again, widening exposure. The owner loses track of who can reach the data.
steps.whenFixed: Automatic guest-access expiry removes stale external access before it spreads far.

outcome.prevented: Re-sharing by external users is blocked, so access stays with the people the owner chose.
outcome.notPrevented: The files spread to an unknown set of outsiders through repeated re-sharing.

title: Guest account holding a directory role
summary: A guest account that was granted a directory role is used to read the directory and hand privileged access to another account.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: A guest account was given a directory role during a project and never removed. The attacker controls that guest account.

steps.title: Sign-in evaluated by Conditional Access
steps.text: The guest signs in through a browser and its role rights come along. Only guest-focused controls treat this account differently from a normal member.

gaps.text: Guest sign-ins are not restricted, so an external account can carry a privileged role.

fix.caTemplate: Restrict guest access with Conditional Access

steps.whenFixed: Blocked: guest access is restricted, so the external account cannot use its role.

steps.title: Directory read
steps.text: The attacker lists users, groups and roles to map the organization. This makes it easy to choose high-value targets.
steps.whenFixed: Guest directory access is restricted, so the account cannot enumerate other users.

steps.title: Another account promoted
steps.text: The attacker adds a second account to a privileged role to keep control if the guest is removed. This creates a standing back door.
steps.whenFixed: The role change is written to the audit log and surfaces for review.

outcome.prevented: Guest restrictions and directory limits stop the external account from reading or escalating.
outcome.notPrevented: The attacker maps the tenant and plants a second privileged account.

title: Legacy authentication mailbox access
summary: An attacker uses an older mail protocol that cannot prompt for MFA to reach a mailbox with a stolen password.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker has the user's password and connects with a legacy protocol that only supports password sign-in. MFA cannot be requested on that path.

steps.title: Sign-in evaluated by Conditional Access
steps.text: The attacker authenticates with a legacy client, which never triggers an MFA prompt. Only blocking legacy authentication closes this path.

gaps.text: Legacy authentication is still allowed, so a password alone reaches the mailbox.

steps.whenFixed: Blocked: legacy authentication is refused, so the password-only client cannot connect.

steps.title: Mailbox downloaded
steps.text: The attacker pulls mail through the legacy protocol, reading recent messages and attachments. The connection looks like an old mail client.
steps.whenFixed: Mailbox auditing records the legacy access for responders.

steps.title: External forwarding turned on
steps.text: The attacker configures mailbox forwarding to an outside address so new mail is copied automatically. Access continues even if the password changes.
steps.whenFixed: External forwarding is blocked and the change raises an alert.

outcome.prevented: Legacy authentication is refused, so the stolen password cannot open the mailbox.
outcome.notPrevented: The attacker reads the mailbox and forwards its mail out of the tenant.

title: Mailbox permission grab
summary: An attacker with admin rights grants itself full access to other users' mailboxes and reads them directly.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker controls an account that can manage mailbox permissions and targets executive mailboxes.

steps.title: Full access granted to a mailbox
steps.text: The attacker gives its own account full access to a target mailbox. No password reset is needed and the owner is not notified.
steps.whenFixed: The permission change is written to the audit log and surfaces for review.

steps.title: Mailbox opened as a delegate
steps.text: The attacker opens the target mailbox using the new access and reads sensitive mail. The activity looks like normal delegate access.
steps.whenFixed: Mailbox auditing records the delegate access so it can be spotted.

outcome.prevented: The permission change is recorded and reviewed before sensitive mail is exposed.
outcome.notPrevented: The attacker reads executive mailboxes directly through delegated access.

title: Mailbox rule exfiltration
summary: An attacker with mailbox access sets up inbox rules and forwarding to copy mail out of the tenant automatically.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker already has access to a user's mailbox and wants a quiet, ongoing copy of incoming mail.

steps.title: Forwarding inbox rule created
steps.text: The attacker creates an inbox rule that forwards new mail to an outside address and hides it in a rarely-seen folder. Mail now leaves the mailbox on arrival.
steps.whenFixed: External forwarding is blocked and the rule creation raises an alert.

steps.title: Mailbox forwarding enabled
steps.text: The attacker also turns on mailbox-level forwarding as a backup path. Even if the rule is removed, copies keep flowing out.
steps.whenFixed: External forwarding is blocked and the outbound spam alert flags the sudden external flow.

outcome.prevented: External forwarding is refused, so no mail leaves the tenant and the attempts are alerted.
outcome.notPrevented: Every incoming message is copied to the attacker for as long as the rules survive.

title: Malicious OAuth app consent
summary: A user is tricked into consenting to a malicious application, which then reads mail and files through the granted permissions.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker sends a convincing link asking the user to grant an application access to their data. The user clicks through the consent screen.

steps.title: Consent granted to the application
steps.text: The user approves the application, which is added to the tenant and receives standing access to mail and files. No password is needed again.
steps.whenFixed: User consent is routed to admin approval, so the malicious app is never granted access.

steps.title: Mail and files read through the app
steps.text: The app reads the user's mailbox and documents using the permissions it was given. The access continues without any further sign-in.
steps.whenFixed: Mailbox auditing records the app's access for responders to review.

outcome.prevented: The consent request is held for admin approval, so the malicious app never gains access.
outcome.notPrevented: The attacker's app reads mail and files quietly for as long as the grant remains.

title: Mass file deletion
summary: A compromised user deletes files across SharePoint and OneDrive at scale to disrupt the business or force a ransom.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker controls a user's account with broad access to document libraries and intends to destroy data.

steps.title: Sign-in evaluated by Conditional Access
steps.text: The attacker signs in from an unmanaged machine before the deletions begin. Strong sign-in controls are the last chance to stop it.

gaps.text: MFA is not enforced, so a stolen password reaches the user's files.

fix.caTemplate: Require multifactor authentication for all users

steps.whenFixed: Blocked: MFA is required, so the stolen password cannot reach the files.

steps.title: Files deleted at scale
steps.text: The attacker deletes large numbers of files across libraries in a short time. Shared workspaces suddenly lose their content.
steps.whenFixed: A mass-deletion alert fires on the burst and each deletion is written to the audit log.

steps.title: Recovery from versions and retention
steps.text: Deleted files and previous versions can be restored for a limited time. Quick detection means most content comes back.
steps.whenFixed: Version history keeps prior copies, so the deleted files can be restored.

outcome.prevented: MFA stops the takeover, so no files are deleted.
outcome.notPrevented: Large numbers of files are deleted, and recovery depends on versioning and retention.

title: Mass group deletion
summary: A compromised administrator deletes many groups, breaking access, mail flow and team membership across the tenant.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker controls an account that can manage groups and wants to disrupt access broadly.

steps.title: Sign-in evaluated by Conditional Access
steps.text: The account signs in from an unfamiliar address before the deletions begin. Strong sign-in controls are the last chance to stop it.

gaps.text: MFA is not enforced, so a stolen password reaches group management.

fix.caTemplate: Require multifactor authentication for all users

steps.whenFixed: Blocked: MFA is required, so the stolen password cannot reach group management.

steps.title: Groups deleted in bulk
steps.text: The attacker deletes many groups, removing the access, distribution lists and teams that depend on them. Users suddenly lose shared resources.
steps.whenFixed: Each deletion is written to the audit log, so the burst is detected quickly.

steps.title: Access lost across services
steps.text: Membership-based access to mail, files and teams disappears with the groups. Microsoft 365 groups can be restored for a limited time.
steps.whenFixed: Prompt detection shortens the outage and allows recovery within the retention window.

outcome.prevented: MFA stops the takeover, so no groups are deleted.
outcome.notPrevented: Access breaks across the tenant until the groups are restored.

title: Mass user deletion
summary: A compromised administrator deletes many user accounts at once to disrupt the business.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker controls an account with user-management rights and intends to cause maximum disruption.

steps.title: Sign-in evaluated by Conditional Access
steps.text: The account signs in from an unfamiliar address before the deletions begin. Strong sign-in controls are the last chance to stop it.

gaps.text: MFA is not enforced, so a stolen password reaches user management.

fix.caTemplate: Require multifactor authentication for all users

steps.whenFixed: Blocked: MFA is required, so the stolen password cannot reach user management.

steps.title: Accounts deleted in bulk
steps.text: The attacker deletes many accounts quickly, cutting off sign-in and mail for those users. The business impact is immediate.
steps.whenFixed: Each deletion is written to the audit log, so the burst is detected quickly.

steps.title: Recovery window
steps.text: Deleted accounts and their data can be restored for a limited time. The faster the burst is noticed, the more can be recovered.
steps.whenFixed: Retention of deleted users' OneDrive data keeps their files recoverable during the window.

outcome.prevented: MFA stops the takeover, so no accounts are deleted.
outcome.notPrevented: Many users lose access at once, and only prompt detection limits the damage.

title: MFA tampering after compromise
summary: After taking over a privileged account, an attacker strips users' MFA and revokes their sessions to lock in control.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker controls a privileged account that can manage other users' authentication methods.

steps.title: Victims' MFA removed
steps.text: The attacker disables strong authentication on target accounts so they can be signed into with passwords alone. This weakens the accounts for later use.
steps.whenFixed: The change is written to the audit log and re-enforced MFA restores protection.

steps.title: Existing sessions revoked
steps.text: The attacker revokes the users' sessions to force fresh sign-ins on the weakened accounts. This helps push out the legitimate users.
steps.whenFixed: The session revocation is written to the audit log and surfaces for review.

steps.title: Attacker registers its own MFA
steps.text: The attacker registers a new authentication method it controls on a target account. This gives durable access under the attacker's own factor.
steps.whenFixed: Method controls limit what can be registered and suspicious-activity reporting flags the change.

outcome.prevented: MFA policy re-enforces protection and every change is recorded and reviewable.
outcome.notPrevented: The attacker holds weakened accounts under its own MFA method.

title: Password spray on an account without MFA
summary: An attacker guesses a common password for an account that has no MFA registered and signs in unchallenged.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker tries a handful of common passwords against many accounts at a slow pace to avoid lockouts. One targeted account has never registered MFA.

steps.title: Sign-in evaluated by Conditional Access
steps.text: A sprayed password matches and the account signs in. With no MFA registered, only password and risk controls stand in the way.

gaps.text: The account has no MFA, so a correct password alone grants access.

fix.caTemplate: Require multifactor authentication for all users

gaps.text: No sign-in risk policy, so the high-risk sign-in is not challenged.

fix.caTemplate: Require multifactor authentication for medium and high sign-in risk

steps.whenFixed: Blocked: MFA is required, so the guessed password alone is not enough.

steps.title: Account explored
steps.text: The attacker reads the mailbox and shared files to learn the business and find more targets. Nothing is changed, so the sign-in looks ordinary.
steps.whenFixed: Mailbox auditing records the access so the takeover can be spotted.

steps.title: Mail forwarded out
steps.text: The attacker creates a rule that forwards new mail to an outside address. This gives quiet, lasting access to the conversation.
steps.whenFixed: External forwarding is blocked and the rule creation raises an alert.

outcome.prevented: MFA and lockout controls stop the guessed password from granting access.
outcome.notPrevented: The attacker takes over the account and forwards its mail out of the tenant.

title: Privilege escalation by role assignment
summary: An attacker who took over an account with role-management rights grants itself higher privileges and plants a back-door application.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker has taken over a help-desk account that can manage group membership and role assignments.

steps.title: Sign-in evaluated by Conditional Access
steps.text: The account signs in from an unfamiliar address at medium risk. Strong sign-in controls are the last chance to stop it before privileges are changed.

gaps.text: MFA is not enforced for this account, so a stolen password reaches role management.

fix.caTemplate: Require multifactor authentication for all users

steps.whenFixed: Blocked: MFA is required, so the stolen password cannot reach role management.

steps.title: Privileged role granted
steps.text: The attacker adds its account to a privileged role, gaining tenant-wide control. The change takes effect immediately.
steps.whenFixed: The role change is written to the audit log and surfaces for review.

steps.title: Back-door application added
steps.text: The attacker registers a hidden application with broad permissions so access survives password and role cleanup. The application acts on its own, without a user present.
steps.whenFixed: Consent and application-credential controls stop the back-door app from being usable.

outcome.prevented: MFA stops the takeover before any role can be changed.
outcome.notPrevented: The attacker gains tenant-wide control and hides a back-door application.

title: Sign-in from outside allowed countries
summary: An attacker signs in from a country the organization never operates in and reaches a user's mailbox and files.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker has the user's password and can approve MFA through a phished prompt. The organization only works from a small set of countries.

steps.title: Sign-in evaluated by Conditional Access
steps.text: The attacker connects from an address in Russia. Only a location control can tell this apart from an ordinary sign-in.

gaps.text: No location policy, so sign-ins from countries the business never uses are allowed.

fix.caTemplate: Block sign-ins from countries outside the allowed list

steps.whenFixed: Blocked: the sign-in comes from a country outside the allowed list and is refused.

steps.title: Mailbox opened and read
steps.text: The attacker reads recent mail and searches for finance and reset messages. The session behaves like the real user, so nothing looks out of place.
steps.whenFixed: Mailbox auditing records the foreign-location access for responders to catch.

steps.title: Mail forwarded outside the tenant
steps.text: The attacker creates an inbox rule that forwards new mail to an external address. Copies now leave the tenant automatically.
steps.whenFixed: External forwarding is blocked and the rule creation raises an alert.

outcome.prevented: The foreign sign-in is refused, so the mailbox is never opened.
outcome.notPrevented: The attacker reads the mailbox and quietly forwards mail out of the tenant.

title: Stolen session token replay
summary: An attacker replays a session token stolen through a fake sign-in page and signs in as the user without re-entering a password or MFA.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker has captured a valid session token from the user through a fake sign-in page that relayed the real one. The token still carries the multifactor approval the user completed.
steps.whenFixed: The Check browser extension recognises the fake sign-in page and blocks it, so no token is captured in the first place.

steps.title: Sign-in evaluated by Conditional Access
steps.text: The attacker replays the token from an unmanaged Windows browser on a hosting-provider address. Because the token already carries MFA, only device and risk controls can still stop the session.

gaps.text: No compliant-device requirement, so a replayed token from any machine is accepted.

fix.caTemplate: Require a compliant or Microsoft Entra hybrid joined device

gaps.text: No sign-in risk policy, so the medium-risk replay is not challenged.

fix.caTemplate: Require multifactor authentication for medium and high sign-in risk

steps.whenFixed: Blocked: the device is not compliant, so the replayed token is refused.

steps.title: Mailbox searched for valuable mail
steps.text: The attacker opens the mailbox and searches for invoices, payroll and password-reset messages. Nothing is changed yet, so the activity looks like normal browsing.
steps.whenFixed: Mailbox auditing records the search, giving responders an early signal of takeover.

steps.title: Forwarding set up for ongoing access
steps.text: The attacker creates an inbox rule and turns on mailbox forwarding so copies of new mail reach an outside address. This keeps the attacker informed even after the token expires.
steps.whenFixed: External forwarding is blocked by policy and the rule creation raises an alert.

outcome.prevented: The replayed token is refused at sign-in because the device is not compliant, and the takeover never starts.
outcome.notPrevented: The attacker reads and quietly forwards mail for as long as the stolen token and forwarding rule survive.

title: Transport-rule exfiltration
summary: An attacker with Exchange admin rights creates an organization-wide transport rule that blind-copies mail to an outside address.

steps.title: Starting assumption
steps.text: The attacker controls an Exchange administrator account and wants to capture mail across the whole organization at once.

steps.title: Organization-wide transport rule created
steps.text: The attacker creates a transport rule that blind-copies messages to an external address for every mailbox. One change captures the entire mail flow.
steps.whenFixed: The rule creation is written to the audit log and surfaces for review.

steps.title: Company mail copied out
steps.text: Mail for all users is now silently copied to the attacker. The volume of external mail rises sharply.
steps.whenFixed: The outbound spam alert flags the surge of external mail so responders can act.

outcome.prevented: The transport-rule change is recorded and the external surge is alerted for fast removal.
outcome.notPrevented: All company mail is copied out of the tenant through a single hidden rule.
